newsitem.title: UK: Britain warns Nigeria over poll system flaws.
newsitem.headline: Britain warns Nigeria over poll system flaws.

text.p: Britain said on Thursday it would not accept a victory by Nigeria's military ruler General Sani Abacha in planned civilian-rule elections next year unless flaws in the poll process were remedied.
"At the moment it is flawed," Tony Lloyd, Foreign Office minister responsible for Africa, told the Financial Times in an interview.

"We know that the process of establishment of political parties has been so one-sided as to guarantee that there will be one serious candidate...(resulting in) the transition of General Abacha to President Abacha. We cannot accept that."
The Financial Times said Lloyd did not close the door on Nigeria's transition programme but made clear a wider registration of parties was one of the reforms necessary.
"The already strained relations with Nigeria, one of Britain's leading trading partners in Africa, are likely to deteriorate further in the light of the minister's comments," said the newspaper.
Britain's new Labour government, which has pledged to put ethics at the heart of foreign policy, hosts talks on Thursday over Nigeria's suspension from the Commonwealth.
The suspension was imposed in 1995 after Nigeria's military-led administration executed writer Ken Saro-Wiwa and eight other minority rights activists despite widespread clemency appeals.

The Commonwealth Ministerial Action Group (CMAG) will spend the day listening to Nigerian opposition groups and human rights organisations to help it decide whether to recommend tougher action by Commonwealth states against Nigeria.

This week's session will gather information for a crunch meeting in September when the eight-nation ministerial group will finalise its recommendation to a Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting (CHOGM), to be held a month later.
The 53-member Commonwealth largely groups members of the former British Empire.
CMAG comprises Britain, Canada, New Zealand, South Africa, Zimbabwe, Ghana, Jamaica and Malaysia.
British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook has already said London would recommend that Nigeria should remain suspended.
Nigeria has protested against the meeting, saying the Commonwealth risked breaking up over the issue.

Foreign Minister Tom Ikimi said on Tuesday that Nigeria felt CMAG could no longer be impartial in its recommendations. Nigeria, Africa's most populous nation, plunged into political turmoil in June 1993 when the army annulled a presidential election despite pledges to restore democracy.

Abacha has promised to hand over to a democratically elected president in 1998. But the opposition is sceptical that this will happen and points to the continued detention of opponents -- among them Moshood Abiola, the presumed winner of the annulled poll.
